Bankrupt
BANK-rupt
n. (a trader who cannot pay his just debts, or who acts to defraud his creditors)
Likely bank-broken, the fund broken, with Latin ruptus, broken. Webster's strict sense is a trader who secretes himself or otherwise tends to defraud his creditors. In the looser sense, a trader unable to pay his just debts. He does not apply the word to every insolvent man.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again: but the righteous sheweth mercy, and giveth. The rich ruleth over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender. Scripture does not use the statute-word. It does name the man whose debts outrun his payment, and it names the wickedness of borrowing with no intent to pay.

A bankrupt, in Webster's strict sense, is a trader. The moral question underneath the statute is older: does the man pay what he owes, or does he hide? Inability is not the same act as fraud. Both can break a fund. Only one is the wickedness of Psalm 37.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): a trader who secretes himself, or does certain other acts tending to defraud his creditors; in a looser sense, a trader unable to pay his just debts. Bankruptcy belongs to traders; insolvency, to other persons.

expand to see more

BANKRUPT, n. A trader who secretes himself, or does certain other acts tending to defraud his creditors.

In a less technical sense, a trader who fails or becomes unable to pay his just debts.

In strictness, no person but a trader can be a bankrupt. Bankruptcy is applied to merchants and traders; insolvency, to other persons.

Key Scripture

Psa 37:21 — "The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again: but the righteous sheweth mercy, and giveth."

Pro 22:7 — "The rich ruleth over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender."

Rom 13:8 — "Owe no man any thing, but to love one another: for he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law."

Modern Corruption

The age uses bankrupt as a sneer for any empty purse, and also as a costume for the man who hides from the debt.

expand to see more

Webster keeps the word on the trader, and he keeps fraud in the strict definition. A failed harvest is not the same as a secreted self. Psalm 37:21 judges the second.

The other corruption is the boast. A man calls himself bankrupt to end the conversation about what he still owes. The borrower remains servant to the lender until the debt is paid or forgiven by the one who holds it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin ruptus, broken. The moral field is the wicked who pays not again (Psa 37:21) and the borrower as servant (Pro 22:7).

expand to see more

The broken bank is the picture. The fund failed. The duty to the creditor did not.

Webster's limit matters. Not every poor man is a bankrupt. The word belongs to trade, and in its strict sense to fraud.

Usage

"The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again — the verse under the strict sense."

"The borrower is servant to the lender — why the name is never a small insult."
